title: A Slam champ at last! Andreeva overpowers Chwalinska to win Roland Garros
description: Touted for years as a future Grand Slam champion, 19-year-old Mirra Andreeva delivered on that promise Saturday, defeating qualifier Maja Chwalinska in straight sets to claim her first Major title at Roland Garros.

body:
Mirra Andreeva is no longer just a teen prodigy. She’s a Grand Slam champion.

The 19-year-old defeated qualifier Maja Chwalinska 6-3, 6-2 in 1 hour and 22 minutes on Court Philippe-Chatrier on Saturday to win her first Roland Garros title, becoming the youngest champion in Paris since Monica Seles in 1992.

"I've been watching Roland Garros on TV since I was very, very young," Andreeva said during the trophy presentation. "It's also a big dream of mine to win this tournament, and I honestly cannot believe that I'm holding this trophy right now."

Like Seles three decades ago, Andreeva has long been touted as the next big thing in women’s tennis. She won her first WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz match at just 15, defeating Leylah Fernandez after receiving a wild card into the Madrid WTA 1000. A few months later, she reached the third round at Roland Garros and the second week at Wimbledon, cementing her status as a generational prospect.

Since then, the milestones have continued to pile up.

Her first title came at Iasi in 2024 and was followed by a silver medal in doubles at the Paris Olympics. In 2025, she became the youngest WTA 1000 champion when she lifted the trophy in Dubai, then backed it up with a title run in Indian Wells, defeating Aryna Sabalenka in the final. Later that year, she made her Top 5 debut.

A historic win for Mirra Andreeva! 👏#RolandGarros pic.twitter.com/f7kEoW1rfW

— wta (@WTA) June 6, 2026

And now, at the site of her first Major semifinal, Andreeva has joined the ranks of the elite women to win a Grand Slam title, and she did so in dominant fashion. The 32nd champion in tournament history, she dropped only 17 games in the second week; only Iga Swiatek (2020, 2024) and Steffi Graf (1988) conceded fewer en route to the Roland Garros crown.

She dropped five games to Jil Teichmann in the fourth round before dispatching No. 18 seed Sorana Cirstea in the quarterfinals and No. 15 seed Marta Kostyuk -- previously 17-0 on clay this season -- in the semifinals, losing just seven games across those two matches. Despite an encouraging start, Chwalinska managed only five games in the final.

Final recap: Andreeva wins 10 of last 12 games in final sprint to title

Whether it was nerves, wind or a combination of both, the match opened with four consecutive breaks in an unusual start to a Grand Slam final. But even then, there was no doubt how badly both players wanted to seize a career-defining moment.

Chwalinska was the first to break the pattern with a love hold for 3-2, but whatever momentum there was to be gained, Andreeva quickly squashed. She finished her first hold in the next game with a backhand winner followed by an ace to draw level at 3-all, the first of four straight games she would win to take the opening set.

She gave Chwalinska a dose of her own medicine with a varied attack, re-upping the velocity on her forehand after slowing it down to start the match and moving forward with confidence, a skill that has increasingly become one of her strengths. She closed the set with a break at love, punctuated by her trademark backhand.

From there, Andreeva’s dominance became too much for Chwalinska, who appeared to feel the physical and mental toll after playing nine matches to reach this point after advancing through qualifying.

Andreeva extended her run to nine straight games to take a 5-0 lead in the second, and while Chwalinska offered brief resistance by taking the next two, it only delayed the inevitable. Not dwelling on the missed chance to serve it out, Andreeva calmly broke at love and sealed her first Grand Slam title with a backhand winner.

WHAT DREAMS ARE MADE OF! 🤩#RolandGarros pic.twitter.com/KvKMt6q24Q

— wta (@WTA) June 6, 2026

"When she won those two games in a row when I was 5-0 up, obviously I was a little bit, you know -- I obviously didn't want to lose those two games, especially the game on my serve," Andreeva said in her post-match press conference. "But I just told myself that it was fine, because I feel like from that side the wind was going forward. So basically, you really couldn't hit as hard as you usually hit.

"I liked the other side better, so I felt like, 'Okay, if this side didn't work, I'll try to win the game on that side.'"

The aftermath: What it all means

For starters, Andreeva is going to need a larger trophy case if she plans to continue at this pace.

Her first Grand Slam marks the sixth singles trophy of her young career, which now includes titles at every level from the 250-tier up. She also has three doubles crowns in addition to her Olympic silver medal. Two of those are WTA 1000 triumphs, matching her two singles titles at that level.

She is tied with Sabalenka for the most titles this season with three.

Perhaps even more notable is that Andreva will overtake Australian Open champion Elena Rybankina and Sabalenka for the No. 1 spot in the Race to the WTA Finals, climbing four places from No. 5. She will also rise two spots to No. 6 in the PIF WTA Rankings on Monday, moving ahead of Elina Svitolina and last year’s Roland Garros champion Coco Gauff.

Of course, that improvement pales in comparison to Chwalinska, who will achieve a career-high ranking of No. 21 after reaching her first Grand Slam final. It’s a career-changing result for the 24-year-old, who had yet to crack the Top 100 when she arrived in Paris in June.

An incredible run Maja! 👏👏👏👏#RolandGarros pic.twitter.com/MzEaY8mrMl

— wta (@WTA) June 6, 2026

By more than doubling her career win total on the WTA Tour, Chwalinska now finds herself in a position to carve out a place on the main circuit with a ranking strong enough to appear in at least one year’s worth of main draws and, more importantly, the next four Grand Slams.

"It will be different, for sure, but I think and I hope that I'll adapt," Chwalinska said during her post-match press conference. "I'm definitely very grateful for this time, but yeah, it's in the past now. So I just need to continue to stay present and give my all to be a better player every day."

A tradition like no other: Andreeva thanks herself on the biggest stage

When Snoop Dogg made his "I want to thank me" speech in 2018, he likely didn’t anticipate inspiring a future Grand Slam champion.

But as has become tradition for Andreeva, who has adopted the positive self-talk model throughout some of the biggest moments of her career, she thanked herself on tennis’ biggest stage after accepting the Suzanne-Lenglen Cup.

ALL OF THE FEELS! 😍#RolandGarros pic.twitter.com/0Qg07XgKEX

— wta (@WTA) June 6, 2026

"Last but not least, I also want to thank myself for believing in myself," Andreeva said. "For always giving 100% even when it’s tough. Trying every day to be better as a person and as a player. Believing that I can do this while fighting so many demons inside of me. Only I know how tough it was for me and how nervous I was throughout these two weeks.

"So thanks to myself for working so hard and giving my best."
